newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German plant, equipment sector sees upturn.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German plant, equipment sector sees upturn.

text.p: Germany's industrial plant and equipment-makers suffered a six percent drop in new orders last year, but 1997 looks brighter due to expected growth in exports and domestic demand, the VDMA association said on Wednesday.

Output grew just one percent in real terms in 1996 but should rise three percent in 1997 as a global economic upturn fuels demand for plant and machinery made in Germany, the industry group said on Wednesday.
The outlook broadly matches a separate forecast made by the car industry on Wednesday which predicted two to three percent growth in car output this year, down from 4.1 percent in 1996.
"The real problem last year was weak domestic investment," VDMA chief economist Herbert Kriegbaum said in a telephone interview.
"We think 1997 will be better, particularly because the world economy is doing better and west Europe is at the start of an economic recovery."

The sector, which builds factories and manufactures industrial machinery, generated annual sales of 235 billion marks ($143.2 billion) last year and employs 945,000 people. Almost 50 percent of German plant and equipment exports go to western Europe.
Kriegbaum predicted exports would grow four percent in 1997 while domestic demand would rise two percent.
The recent weakening of the mark against the dollar and European currencies should boost the sector's ability to compete internationally by making its products cheaper abroad, he added.

Kriegbaum said the VDMA also had reason to hope for a pick-up in domestic investment as interest rates were low, wage deals for 1997 were moderate and mounting exports should raise capacity usage in exporting industries, prompting firms to buy new machinery.
"We expect that over the year the upturn in exports will throw a spark onto domestic investment," Kriegbaum said.
The sector's predicted output rise of three percent exceeds forecasts for overall gross domestic product (GDP) growth which range from 2.0 to 2.5 percent.

Kriegbaum said that in 1996, domestic plant and equipment orders fell nine percent while orders from abroad fell four percent. Foreign order levels remained "quite acceptable" while domestic order levels were modest, Kriegbaum said.
He said the foreign order inflow was held back last year by the after-effects of the mark's appreciation in 1995 and by weak economic growth in western Europe.
"Domestically, investment activity stagnated but deliveries weren't that badly affected thanks to an order overhang from 1995," Kriegbaum said.

The VDMA earlier reported a 13 percent fall in incoming orders year-on-year in December but added this was mainly due to Christmas and New Year falling between weekends which prompted many businesses to shut up shop on December 20.
